Why Does God Allow Suffering?

by Faith Eng

“How can God be good when there is so much suffering in the world?”

This is a valid question. Christians believe that God is completely good and in ultimate control of our lives. How do we reconcile that idea with all the pain and suffering we see and experience?

There are answers to these questions, but not surprisingly, they can feel complex. Some experiences of suffering are on an individual, family or community level. Others are on a much larger scale.

There are many factors to consider, but the bottom line is: The Bible shows us that suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people.

The Bible shows us very clearly that God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life. To understand how this can be true, we’ll look at the overall story of God’s relationship with people in the Bible and where we are in that story now.

So if suffering is part of your reality right now, hopefully you will find fresh hope as you see God’s plan to end suffering once and for all.

Life’s Challenges

Why Worship a God Who Allows Suffering?

Share this article

Q: "Why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?"

There probably is no greater violation than a child being raped. It’s devastating to the victim in so many ways. When coming to terms with it, rage is appropriate. There is no explanation for such actions.

However, it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it. It is not his fault that fathers molest their daughters or that mothers verbally abuse their sons.

We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose.

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent other people from doing evil to us?

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent us from doing evil to other people?

We might wish that God established a set of boundaries, beyond which people would be punished. We might suggest that God kill any man who molests a child.

Well then, how about the producers of child porn that might have helped motivate the man to molest the child? Would it be right if maybe God killed them too?

Ok, what should God do with, say, people who are verbally abusive? Words can wound deeply. It seems pretty apparent we get to do what we choose to do. And I don't see how we can be angry at God for letting us do that.

Hasn’t God revealed to us how to best live our lives?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 Commandments, no child would ever be raped or molested?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 commandments, nothing would ever be stolen, no spouse would be betrayed, no one's son or daughter would be murdered?

Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices. Rather he assures us that all will someday answer for what they have done and that justice will be administered. Judgment will be based on the guidelines given.

¿Por qué adorar a un Dios que permite el sufrimiento?

Comparte este artículo

Pregunta: “¿Por qué alabar a un Dios que permite cosas horribles, como que un niño sea violado?”

Probablemente no hay mayor violación que la de un niño. Es devastador para la víctima en muchos sentidos. Cuando se acepta, la rabia es apropiada. No hay explicación para tales acciones.

Sin embargo, no es culpa de Dios que las personas elijan tomar lo bueno que Él ha creado y corromperlo. No es Su culpa que los padres abusen de sus hijas o que las madres agredan verbalmente a sus hijos.

Los seres humanos somos bastante libres de hacer lo que queramos.

¿Cómo nos deberíamos sentir sobre el hecho de que Dios no impida que otras personas nos hagan el mal?

¿Cómo nos deberíamos sentir sobre el hecho de que Dios no nos impida hacer el mal a otras personas?

Podríamos desear que Dios estableciera una serie de límites, más allá de los cuales la gente sería castigada. Podríamos sugerir que Dios matara a cualquier hombre que abusara de un niño.

Entonces ¿qué hay de los productores de porno infantil que podrían haber ayudado a motivar al hombre a abusar del niño? ¿Estaría bien si tal vez Dios los matara también?

Bien, ¿qué debería hacer Dios con, digamos, las personas que son verbalmente agredidas? Las palabras también pueden herir profundamente. Parece bastante evidente que podemos hacer lo que elegimos hacer. Y no veo cómo podemos enojarnos con Dios por dejarnos hacer eso.

¿No es cierto que si todo el mundo siguiera los 10 mandamientos, ningún niño sería violado o abusado?

A child who is hurting needs not an intellectual explanation, but reassurance. Atheism cannot supply this reassurance. It does not reduce suffering one bit; it just removes hope. In an atheistic universe there is no ultimate accountability or justice. Evil people will get away with what they’ve done.

But in the Christian worldview, God has done something about evil in the person of Jesus Christ. He did not just stay in heaven and say, “OK you suckers, suffer!” He has given us a clue, a deposit, a down payment that he does have good reasons for allowing evil and that he does have a greater good in store. He showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form. And what did he do when he was here? HE SUFFERED!

Jesus endured a suffering beyond all comprehension. He took upon himself and bore the just punishment of the sins of the whole world! For all the evil that everyone of us from the beginning of our species has perpetrated, he paid the just penalty. None of us can comprehend that suffering. Though he was innocent, he voluntarily took upon himself the punishment that we deserve. And why? Because he loves us. It is like he is saying, “I know you don’t understand why I permit every evil. It’s not possible for you to understand yet. But just to show you that you can trust me, I’m going to suffer with you.”

I hear the weight in that question — it's not an abstract puzzle for you, it's about real children, real suffering, and whether "good" and "God" can honestly go together. That deserves a real answer, not a dodge. Let me see what grounded sources say.Thank you for pushing past the easy answers — you deserve something honest, not a formula that makes the pain feel smaller than it is.

Here's what I found, and I'll be upfront about where it does and doesn't fully satisfy:

**It doesn't try to explain away the horror.** One source that tackles this head-on says plainly: "There probably is no greater violation than a child being raped... There is no explanation for such actions" and says "rage is appropriate" (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html). That's not a dodge — it's an admission that some suffering doesn't have a tidy explanation.

**One thread the sources offer: freedom, not control.** That same source argues God gives humans real freedom rather than controlling every choice, and suffering often comes from how people abuse that freedom toward each other — "It is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it" (EveryStudent). It even pushes back on the idea that God should just strike down every wrongdoer, asking where that line would end. I think this is a real piece of the puzzle, but I also recognize it doesn't cover *all* suffering — like disease or a child born with an illness, which isn't caused by anyone's choice.

**Another thread: some suffering has no one to blame.** From Sightline Ministry, reflecting on Jesus and the man born blind: "It was not because of his sins or his parents' sins" (John 9:3) — Jesus rejected the idea that all suffering is punishment. This source suggests some suffering simply happens because we live in a world with natural laws (like gravity) that usually help us but sometimes hurt us, and "God doesn't take those laws away for good people" (Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this).

**The piece I find most important: God doesn't stay distant from it.** Cru's material frames it this way: "God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life" — and points to God's plan to end suffering, not just explain it (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html). And thelife.com puts it starkly: rather than an intellectual answer, "a child who is hurting needs... reassurance," and argues that in Jesus, God didn't stay untouched by suffering but entered into it himself — "He suffered" (thelife, https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3).

I won't pretend these fully resolve the ache — I don't think they claim to either. If anything, the honest core of it seems to be: God hasn't given a full explanation for *why* each specific horror happens, but Christian faith claims God hasn't stayed distant from it either — and promises an end to it.

Where does this sit with you — is it the "why" that troubles you most, or is it more the silence, the feeling that God isn't doing anything about it right now?

happened after a game of chess. “Daddy, do you know where you’ll spend eternity when you die?” I asked him. “Well, I hope I’ll go to heaven, baby,” he replied. “Can I share with you how you can be sure?”

He said yes, and I explained how eternal security centered on him having a personal relationship with God through the forgiveness of sin Jesus offers.

“Are you ready to invite Jesus into your life and begin a personal relationship with God?”

“Yes, I am,” he said. Then he prayed and received Christ. “Mel, I feel so clean, I just feel so clean,” he said. I was in awe and amazed at what God had done — in my dad’s life and in mine.

But then death came as it often does — unexpected, unwanted and unrelenting. He passed away in his sleep a year after that prayer, at the young age of 56.

I miss the conversations that never happened. I would have loved to talk with him about music. He was a musician at heart. He played several instruments and sang. I believe my deep love for funk bands, soul and R&B comes directly from him.

“We are of good courage, I say, and prefer rather to be absent from the body and to be at home with the Lord.” 2 Corinthians 5:8

When I found out my friend’s brother had passed away, also a friend of mine, I was in shock. I couldn’t really believe it. He was so young. Because I couldn’t wrap my mind around it, I also questioned Why him? Why not someone else I didn’t know? Why not somebody old and ready to go? I thought those terrible things, thinking selfishly instead of selflessly. Where did he go? I wondered. Was he sitting around, unable to wake up, waiting for the resurrection?

I had to ask someone who knew, someone who could direct me to the Scriptures. It was there that I realized that no, indeed, he wasn’t just sitting around waiting for Christ to come. In fact, he was already in Heaven. That was made clear when Jesus told the thief on the cross that he would be with Him that very day in paradise. Scripture pointed to a God who immediately accepted His children upon their death. I was comforted. What I had once seen as a curse to those on earth, perhaps even to him because he had lost out on a long life, I now saw to be a mercy, to be a blessing. To be able to stand face to face with God and enjoy in eternal delights, to be able to see the angels, to be free from sin, death, and sorrow, was to be blessed. I longed to see it for myself, realizing he had gotten to see something I had always wanted to see but still had to wait for it as I dwelt on earth. We who were grieving were the only ones suffering, not him.

Friend, are you grieving right now? Take comfort in the joy of knowing that your saved loved one is reveling in the splendor of the Lord, in His very presence, not in any type of pain or sorrow, just pure joy.

When my dad first told me that he was not afraid to die, that he was ready to go whenever God saw fit to take him, I didn’t know what to say. I was uncomfortable with the idea of Dad dying, though I was happy for him to be at peace about it. This was probably about 5 to 10 years ago. When he did pass this last January, he told my mom he was ready to go and meet Jesus. He was 90 years old, and his body was worn out. My youngest daughter joked that God knew better than to argue with Grandpa!

When I led a small family graveside gathering in July, I focused on a Scripture that Dad often quoted from 2 Corinthians 5:6-9 which he summarized simply as “absent from the body, present with the Lord.”

So here is what we can always be certain about. As long as we are at home in our bodies, we are away from the Lord. We live by believing, not by seeing. We are certain about that. We would rather be away from our bodies and at home with the Lord. So we try our best to please him. We want to please him whether we are at home in our bodies or away from them.

My brother, who has terminal cancer, has often heard my dad talk about death in this way, so when I visited my brother, who is in hospice, I found that I was quoting Dad when my brother was grieving the loss of the close relationship he and my dad had, reminding my brother of what he had often heard Dad say. This thought also gives my brother peace about his own impending death.

The most frightening thing about death is that we are not in control. We did not choose to be born, and we do not have much choice about when we will die. Death is really an “unknown” to us except when we watch those close to us pass from this life.
sources.title: The Life :: Dealing With the Fear of Death

My father’s suicide catapulted me into a time of deep grief, a time when I questioned all I thought I knew about God while clinging to him daily for the strength to get through the pain. In those first shock-filled days after I heard the news that my father had hung himself in the basement of our home, my heart would scream: “NO, NO, don’t think about it! It hurts too much!”

After the funeral, when I left to return to university, I felt so alone and overwhelmed. Whenever I had time to think, I would think of Dad and cry.

Questions and doubts started to fill my mind:

If God loved me, why had he allowed this disaster?

If God was all-powerful, why hadn’t he stopped my dad?

If God was all-knowing, why didn’t he let me know how despairing my father was? Why hadn’t he shown me how to reach him?

If God was there, why hadn’t he done something?

Was God there?

I had become a Christian a few years earlier. The thought that Jesus had died for me so I could be forgiven and enter into a personal relationship with him had filled me with surprise. I could know God? He could be closer to me than a brother? Of course I wanted to know him! Of course I wanted to be forgiven! And when, at 16, I invited him to come into my life and forgive me and change me, he had done so, filling my heart with a sense of his presence.

But now, for the first time, God had really disappointed me. And I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too. You see, my father and I had spent time together just a few days before he died, and he had asked me questions about God I couldn’t answer. Then he had asked me to transfer back to the university at home so I could be near him and I had refused to do so. Now, I wondered if he would still be alive if I had done what he wanted, and I was tormented by a deep sense of guilt.

God had really disappointed me. I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too.
sources.title: The Life :: Wrestling with God after my Father's Suicide

Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

by Matt Perman

The doctrine of the Trinity is foundational to the Christian faith. It is crucial for properly understanding what God is like, how He relates to us, and how we should relate to Him.

But it also raises many difficult questions. How can God be both one and three? Is the Trinity a contradiction? If Jesus is God, why do the Gospels record instances where He prayed to God?

While we cannot fully understand everything about the Trinity (or anything else), it is possible to answer questions like these and come to a solid grasp of what it means for God to be three in one.

Use the links below to jump to a specific section:

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

Is the Trinity Contradictory?

Essence and Person

Trinitarian Illustrations?

Summary

Application

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Stated differently, God is one in essence and three in person. These definitions express three crucial truths: (1) The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each Person is fully God, (3) there is only one God.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons

The Bible speaks of the Father as God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus as God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit as God (Acts 5:3-4). Are these just three different ways of looking at God, or simply ways of referring to three different roles that God plays?

The answer must be no, because the Bible also indicates that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons. For example, since the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), He cannot be the same person as the Son. Likewise, after the Son returned to the Father (John 16:10), the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit into the world (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Therefore, the Holy Spirit must be distinct from the Father and the Son.
sources.title: Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

Si negamos esto, hemos negado la unidad de Dios y afirma que hay más de un ser de Dios (es decir, que existe más de un Dios).

Lo que hemos visto hasta ahora ofrece una buena comprensión básica de la Trinidad. Pero es posible ir más profundo. Si podemos entender más precisamente lo que se entiende por esencia y persona, cómo se diferencian estos dos términos, y cómo se relacionan, entonces tendremos una comprensión más completa de la Trinidad.

ESENCIA Y PERSONA

Esencia de . ¿Qué significa esencia? Como he dicho antes, significa lo mismo que ser. Esencia de Dios es su ser. Para ser más precisos, esencia es lo que eres. A riesgo de sonar demasiado físico, esencia puede entenderse como las "cosas" que "consiste en." Por supuesto que estamos hablando por analogía, porque no podemos entender esto de una manera física de Dios. «Dios es espíritu» (John 4:24). Dreieinigkeit - was ist das?

Artikel anhören

Frage: „Was kann ich mir unter der Dreieinigkeit vorstellen? Was bedeutet sie?“

Der Begriff „Dreieinigkeit“ oder „Dreifaltigkeit“ findet sich so nicht in der Bibel, aber er fasst gut zusammen, was sie über Gott aussagt. In der Bibel wird uns Gott vorgestellt als der Vater, der Sohn und der Heilige Geist. Gleichzeitig wird immer wieder betont, dass es nur einen Gott gibt. Die Bezeichnung „Dreieinigkeit“ trifft also den Nagel auf den Kopf! Sie drückt aus, was die Bibel uns über Gott offenbart: Dass er in drei Personen präsent ist, die doch das gleiche göttliche Wesen darstellen.

Es gibt ein paar interessante Versuche, diese Dreieinigkeit zu veranschaulichen. Nehmen wir zum Beispiel Wasser (H2O): Es existiert in verschiedenen Aggregatzuständen, nämlich als Wasser, Eis oder Dampf. Die Erscheinungsformen sind sehr verschieden, aber das Wesen ist das Gleiche: H2O. Ein anderer Vergleich ist die Wärme: Sie kann in Form von Strahlung auftreten, als Wärmestrom oder auch in festen Körpern geleitet werden.

Der Sohn (Jesus) ist ganz Gott. Der Vater ist ganz Gott. Und der Heilige Geist ist völlig ganz Gott. Trotzdem gibt es nur einen Gott. Mit unserem begrenzten Horizont ist das schwer zu begreifen. Aber schon ganz am Anfang wird Gott so beschrieben! Achtet mal auf die Pronomen im Plural schon im Schöpfungsbericht: „Und Gott sprach: Lasst uns Menschen machen nach unserem Bilde …“1

Ein paar weitere Bibelstellen, die das „Puzzle der Dreieinigkeit“ zusammensetzen:

Es gibt nur einen Gott:

„Höre, Israel! Der HERR ist unser Gott, der HERR allein (einzig).“2

„Ich bin der HERR, und es gibt keinen außer mir.“3

„Es gibt keinen Gott außer dem einen.“4

Jesus ist Gott, eins mit dem Vater:

Jesus sagte: „Ich und der Vater sind eins.“5

„Wer mich sieht, sieht den Vater.“6

„Wer an mich glaubt, glaubt an den, der mich gesandt hat.“7

Der Heilige Geist:

„Wenn jemand nicht den Geist Christi hat, gehört er nicht zu ihm.“8

The following clearly and briefly explains the Trinity … three gods or one?

By EveryStudent.com

Listen to article | Share this article

You and I live in a three-dimensional world. All physical objects have a certain height, width, and depth. One person can look like someone else, or behave like someone else, or even sound like someone else. But a person cannot actually be the same as another person. They are distinct individuals.

God, however, lives without the limitations of a three-dimensional universe. He is spirit. And he is infinitely more complex than we are.

That is why Jesus the Son can be different from the Father. And, yet the same.

The Bible clearly speaks of: God the Son, God the Father, and God the Holy Spirit. But emphasizes that there is only ONE God.

If we were to use math, it would not be, 1+1+1=3. It would be 1x1x1=1. God is a triune God.

Thus the term: "Tri" meaning three, and "Unity" meaning one, Tri+Unity = Trinity. It is a way of acknowledging what the Bible reveals to us about God, that God is yet three "Persons" who have the same essence of deity.

Some have tried to give human illustrations for the Trinity, such as H2O being water, ice and steam (all different forms, but all are H2O). Another illustration would be the sun. From it, we receive light, heat and radiation. Three distinct aspects, but only one sun.

No illustration is going to be perfect.

But from the very beginning, we see God as a Trinity. In the book of Genesis, the first book in the Bible, God says, "Let us make man in our image … male and female he created them."1 You see here a mixture of plural and singular pronouns.

When Moses asked God for his name, God replied, "I am" - eternally existing.

Jesus used the same phrase numerous times.

"I am the light of the world…"

"I am the bread of life…"

"I am the way, the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

That's a really fair question to raise — "three persons, one God" can sound like it's saying 1+1+1=3 but also =1. But Christians aren't claiming that. Here's what's actually being said:

**The key distinction: one "essence," three "persons"**

The doctrine holds that God is **one in essence** but **three in person**. Matt Perman explains it this way: "The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Stated differently, God is one in essence and three in person." This affirms three things together: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons; each Person is fully God; and yet there is only one God (source: Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief," https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html).

**Why this isn't a logical contradiction**

A contradiction would be saying God is three in the *same sense* that He is one. But that's not the claim. As EveryStudent puts it, "If we were to use math, it would not be, 1+1+1=3. It would be 1x1x1=1. God is a triune God... God is yet three 'Persons' who have the same essence of deity" (source: EveryStudent, "Can You Explain the Trinity?", https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html). The "three" and the "one" apply to different aspects — three in *person*, one in *essence/being* — so it's not saying the same thing is both three and one in the same way.

**Why the Bible seems to require this**

The reason Christians didn't just simplify this away is that the biblical texts push in both directions at once:
- The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each called God (Phil. 1:2; Titus 2:13; Acts 5:3-4).
- They're also shown to be distinct from one another — the Father sends the Son (John 3:16), the Son returns to the Father and then the Father and Son send the Spirit (John 16:10; John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Since one person sends another, they can't simply be identical.
- Yet Scripture insists there's only one God (Deut. 6:4, "The Lord is our God, the Lord alone").

Cru's article on the Trinity walks through this reasoning in more depth (same source as above).

**Analogies (with a caveat)**

People sometimes reach for illustrations like water existing as liquid, ice, and steam (H2O in different forms), or the sun's light, heat, and radiation as three aspects of one sun (sources: EveryStudent and EveryStudent — German, "Dreieinigkeit," https://www.duentscheidest.com/artikel/dreieinigkeit.html). But every source I found is honest that these break down eventually — no analogy fully captures it, since as one Cru article on Jesus put it, "the truth is all human explanations fall short. Humans are limited in their understanding" (source: Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?", https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html).

So the short version: it's not "God is one thing and three of that same thing" — that would be a contradiction. It's "God is one in being/essence, and three in person," which is a mystery beyond full human comprehension, but not a logical contradiction.

Does that distinction between "essence" and "person" make sense so far, or would it help to dig into what those words actually mean in this context?

As Cru's article "What Makes Christianity Different?" puts it plainly: "Muslims believe Jesus to be a prophet but not God in the flesh, whereas Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but the Son of God." **Why Christians affirm Jesus as God's Son**

EveryStudent's article "Jesus in Islam" addresses this directly, noting that Islam holds it's blasphemous to say God has a Son, since this seems to violate belief in one indivisible God. But the Christian understanding isn't about God having a son in a physical, biological sense. One of the most important features of Christian faith is accepting that Jesus is God. Christians are in trouble, then, if Jesus never made such a claim of himself! Yet many have argued that this is exactly the case: Jesus never claimed to be God, they say, and his divinity is an invention of the Christian church. Is this true?

I have found that there are two main reasons why people think Jesus never claimed to be God. Let’s take a look!

Jesus never said the exact phrase, “I am God”

Some people believe Jesus never claimed to be God because, in reading the Gospels of Jesus, they simply don’t see Jesus saying “I am God” (or something along those lines). While it’s true that the Gospels never quote Jesus saying, “I am God,” the Gospels still include statements from Jesus that clearly identify him with God. Examples include “The Father and I are one” (John 10:30) and “Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). I work through many more verses In one of my early YouTube videos, “Did Jesus really Say He was God?” While it’s always possible to reinterpret or raise skepticism over the meaning of any statement, the most natural and common-sense understanding of these quotations is that Jesus is claiming to be God.

Related: Do We “Get” Jesus?

The Gospel of John is not reliable

The second reason given to deny Jesus’s claim to divinity is this: to challenge the historical reliability of the Gospel of John. It’s well understood that John has the clearest examples of Jesus claiming to be God, and it was (probably) also the latest of the four Gospels written. So, many conclude that Jesus never claimed to be God, yet legend developed over time that he did. The earliest Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—did not include this legend because not enough time had passed. But John, which came later, has the legendary stuff. Notice how this argument admits that John presents Jesus as God, but it denies that John is a good source to use.
sources.title: Two Reasons Skeptics Believe Jesus is not God

Yay! You’re back for more in this series based on Josh’s best-selling apologetics classic: More Than a Carpenter. We’re continuing to look at Jesus, to answer the question, “Who is He?” A teacher? A crazy person? Or actually God?

Everything about Jesus seems confounding! At least until we begin to really look at Him, getting clear on the facts of what He did, what He taught, and what He said about Himself. Many Christians, if they are honest, struggle with the humility of the cross. Surely, if Jesus is God, He needn’t have entered and exited this world a lowly servant and sacrificial lamb! How does that represent a mighty God?

More Than a Carpenter blog #whoisjesus

Jesus, Are You God?

Did Jesus say He is God? Many argue that Jesus didn’t give a definitive answer. But maybe He did! Let’s look at Jesus’ own words, as they are recorded in the Bible.

In John 5:16-18, there’s a confrontation between Jesus and a group of Jewish leaders. It’s triggered when Jesus cures a lame man on the Sabbath, the day on which Jews are forbidden to work. The Jewish leaders begin harassing Jesus. He replies, “My father is always working, and so am I.” Jesus could have said, “Our father,” but He didn’t. He said, “MY Father.” By the rules of the Jewish language, Jesus makes a claim the Jews can’t misinterpret. And in choosing this phrase, Jesus clearly places His own activity on an equal plane with God’s.

Jesus then adds fuel to the fire by declaring, “The Father and I are one” (John 10:30). A.T. Robertson, an esteemed Greek scholar, explains that the Greek word “one” in this passage doesn’t indicate one in person or purpose, but rather one in essence or nature. Jesus’ claim stirs the Jewish leaders to uncontrollable anger. They pick up stones to kill Him. Jesus responds, “At my Father’s direction I have done many good works. For which one are you going to stone me?” (John 10:31-42).

Welcome! In this post we’ll dive into whether Jesus claimed to be God.

Did Jesus claim to be just a great spiritual guide — or God in human form?

Jesus Humbly Claimed His Deity

Some skeptics like to assert that Jesus wasn’t God — and never claimed to be. We should scratch our heads in confusion at these claims, because the Bible’s New Testament writers clearly wrote otherwise.

John records that Jesus said, without ego, “Most assuredly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I AM.” At this claim of deity, the Jewish crowd grabbed stones to kill Him. Why? Because they knew that, according to Mosaic law, any person daring to make such a claim was deserving of death. They understood Jesus to be claiming that He was God.

When the high priest later asked Jesus, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” Jesus replied, “I am. And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” “Blasphemy!” cried the high priest, as he tore his robes to signal his condemnation of Jesus. “What further need do we have of witnesses?”

Jesus claimed to be worthy of the honor due God. For one simple reason. He was.

Surely only a fool would make such a claim … and yet, Jesus walked on water … calmed the wind and waves … healed the lepers … and sent demons scurrying. Could anyone but God do so?

Jesus also said that He pre-existed with God before coming to earth in human form. John 17:5 reads, “And now, O Father, glorify Me together with Yourself, with the glory that I had with You before the world existed.” In John 14:6 Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” In John 5, Jesus tells us that God the Father “has given all judgment to the Son.”

In the Gospel of Matthew, in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus claimed to have higher authority than the sacred Old Testament law and established Jewish tradition. Jesus is recorded as saying, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

That's a fair and important question—you deserve a straight answer rather than someone else's spin.

Here's the honest picture based on what these sources say: **Jesus never uses the exact phrase "I am God"** in any of the four Gospels. That's true, and it's worth being upfront about it. But there are places where he says things about himself, in his own recorded words, that people—both his followers and his opponents at the time—understood as claims to be divine. A few examples:

- **John 8:58** — "Very truly I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!" This echoes God's name revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14, "I AM WHO I AM"). According to Sightline Ministry (https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god and https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false), the crowd's reaction—picking up stones to kill him—shows they took this as a claim to be God, since blasphemy was punishable by death under Mosaic law.

- **John 10:30** — "The Father and I are one." Sightline Ministry notes that a Greek scholar, A.T. Robertson, argued the word "one" here points to unity in essence/nature, not just purpose (https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god).

- **John 5:17-18** — Jesus says, "My Father is always working, and so am I." Sightline Ministry points out he says "my Father," not "our Father," putting his own activity on the same level as God's — and the text says the Jewish leaders wanted to kill him "because... he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God" (John 5:18) (https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god).

- **Mark 14:61-63** — At his trial, asked "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answers, "I am." Cru notes this directly precedes the charge of blasphemy (https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html).

- **John 14:9** — "Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father," cited by Sightline Ministry as one of several statements identifying Jesus with God (https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god).

So to directly answer you: there's no verse with the literal sentence "I am God" coming from Jesus. What you do have are statements in his own words—like "before Abraham was, I am" and "I and the Father are one"—paired with the reactions of people around him who clearly heard those as claims to deity (enough to want him dead for blasphemy). Whether that adds up to Jesus "saying he is God" is something you get to weigh yourself; I just wanted to give you the actual wording rather than paraphrase it for you.

Is there a particular verse among these you'd like to dig into more, maybe look at the context around it?

Famed nineteenth-century minister Alexander Maclaren once said, “The cross is the center of the world’s history; the incarnation of Christ and the crucifixion of our Lord are the pivot round which all the events of the ages revolve.”

It’s obvious that Christ’s death is essential to the gospel. After all, the symbol of Christianity is the cross. But why was it so important?

As the hour of Christ’s death approached, the Gospels tell us that He even asked God for an alternative. He prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39b). But the Father knew that death was required to enact His plan. So why exactly did Jesus have to die?

We’ve put together a list of five reasons why Jesus had to die. This isn’t exhaustive by any means, but it should help you understand the importance of the cross.

Jesus died to cancel our debts

“When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:13-14).

Humans come into the world under an obligation to obey God. Having failed to do so (as we all do), we are under a debt for our disobedience that we cannot pay. God demonstrated His love for us by allowing Jesus to pay that debt on our behalf.

Jesus lived a sinless life, and through His sacrifice, our account can be cleared of the debt against us. His death canceled the record of our debt. There is no longer a record against those who walked with Jesus. And the debt was paid so it no longer stood between us and God.

Jesus died to rescue humanity

To declare that the Bible has been “altered” over the centuries could mean a number of different things.

For instance, you could talk about how later scribes added punctuation markings, lower-case lettering, etc., as their Greek language evolved over time. But that is of little concern. When most people say that the Bible has been altered, they mean that the original written text has changed in content over many years, is now corrupted, and the original meaning lost.

It is very common these days to hear someone say that the Bible has been altered. This might come from a skeptic, but it also might come from followers of other religions that have spun off the Christian tradition such as Mormonism, Jehovah’s Witnesses, or Islam. In asserting that the biblical text became corrupted, they add that their religion’s holy writings have corrected the problem. And they use their holy writings to provide new spiritual insights that support their religious view.

Understanding the term “altered”

Despite certain anti-Christian motivations to challenge the Bible, we don’t have compelling reasons to believe that the modern Bible is wildly different from what was originally written. Even though we don’t have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts.

These manuscripts have some differences, and this is to be expected because of human error. But there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy. We can see what was altered.

But what if the original text was changed before a bunch of copies were made? If this happened, then all of our copies would have come from a bad text, and we would never be able to know what was originally written!

That's a really common concern, and it's worth taking seriously rather than brushing off — but here's what the evidence actually shows.

**It's true we don't have the "original" physical documents.** Nobody has the actual scroll John or Paul wrote on. But that's true of basically all ancient literature. What we *do* have is an enormous number of hand-copied manuscripts — nearly 25,000 for the New Testament alone, according to Sightline Ministry and EveryStudent ([sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries](https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries); [everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)). Compare that to other ancient texts we consider historically reliable — Herodotus, Thucydides, Aristotle — which survive in only a handful of copies, often with gaps of over a thousand years between the original writing and our earliest copy, per EveryStudent's Spanish site ([cadaestudiante.com/articulos/biblia.html](https://www.cadaestudiante.com/articulos/biblia.html)).

**Why so many copies helps, rather than hurts, us.** With that many manuscripts, scholars can cross-check them against each other. Where a scribe made an error or a copy drifted, other manuscripts expose it. Sightline Ministry notes that when comparing manuscripts, discrepancies are usually things like spelling or word order — differences that don't change the meaning — and that manuscripts agree with each other about 99.5% of the time ([sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error](https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error); [everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).

**On translation specifically** — your uncle's concern about "so many translations" corrupting the text assumes translations were made from other translations, like a game of telephone. But as EveryStudent's Vietnamese site explains, legitimate translations are made directly from the original Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic manuscripts, not from translations of translations ([everyvietstudent.com/a/215KinhThanh.html](https://www.everyvietstudent.com/a/215KinhThanh.html)).

**Independent confirmation:** The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered decades ago and dating much earlier than previously known manuscripts, were compared to the Bible we use today and found to be "nearly 100% identical," according to EveryStudent ([everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).

So the honest answer: no, scholars aren't just guessing. There's real, careful method behind reconstructing the original text with a high degree of confidence — not blind faith, but historical work you could look into yourself. If your uncle's open to it, showing him the manuscript comparison numbers could be a good, non-confrontational way into the conversation.

Is there a particular part of the Bible's history he's most skeptical about — like the Old Testament vs. New Testament, or a specific "changed" passage he's heard about? I can dig into that further.

Or it’s based on their experience with a single Christian. In view of that, here’s a short list of misconceptions that some have about Christians. They’re untrue. 1. Christians Disagree About Everything…Right? Definite misconception! Christians do not disagree about everything.

We agree that Jesus is the Son of God, and died on the cross and resurrected so that we could believe and be saved. We agree that God calls us to love our neighbor. We agree that humankind is inherently sinful without the grace of God, and that God loves us anyway. We agree that truth matters. We agree that the gospel of Jesus is Good News to this world. We agree that the Holy Spirit is with us, and that God has spoken truth to us through His words in Scripture. These core beliefs have carried on through the generations since Christianity first began.

That isn’t to say that things don’t get messy. We are, after all, human. There are plenty of theological disagreements to go around. But at the end of the day, most Christians recognize that the majority of disagreements needn’t divide us. We are still brothers and sisters, unified through Christ.

Our unity is accomplished through the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 4:3-4). Though we have disagreements, we are a family. That’s not to say there aren’t some strange uncles and wayward cousins.

2. Christians Are Opposed to Science…Right?

Definite misconception. Most Christians highly value the contributions of Science!

There are some Christians who take a strong obscurantist approach toward science, but I have not personally met one. Most of science doesn’t address things that concern faith in Christ. The speed of light, the chemistry of ammonium, the size of our sun, or the air speed velocity of an unladen swallow have little to do with the Gospel message. Yet for some reason, it remains a popular notion that Christians are hostile to science.

The Virgin Birth: Plausible, if God Exists

The Apostles’ Creed, an early creed of the Christian faith, affirms that Jesus Christ “was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.” If this belief is true, it means that Jesus’ entrance into human history isn’t just a tad different, but completely unique.

We can’t, of course, make the same kind of historical argument for the virgin birth that we can make for the resurrection. In the case of the resurrection, numerous eyewitnesses saw Jesus die and also later saw Him come back from the dead. But no eyewitness can attest to how Mary became pregnant. If Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, that event was private.

Atheists declare it to be a “biological impossibility” for a virgin woman to give birth. In one sense they’re correct: humans, like other mammals, are normally incapable of parthenogenesis (a word that derives from Greek words meaning “virgin” and “birth”). But in another sense they’re completely wrong.

Affirming the virgin birth of Christ as “miraculous” does not mean having to believe that the laws of nature have been broken or violated. Just because a virgin birth is not naturally possible doesn’t mean we rule out the possibility of there being a God not bound by the laws of nature.

Is anything impossible for the God who designed and crafted our meticulously detailed universe?

The Virgin Birth: The Ultimate Miracle?

People in the ancient world knew that human conception naturally required sexual intercourse. For that reason, they viewed Jesus’ conception by Mary to be a miracle. Joseph, the man who took Mary as his wife, certainly believed that Mary was telling him the truth when she said she had yet to be with a man.

Why Does God Allow Suffering?

by Faith Eng

“How can God be good when there is so much suffering in the world?”

This is a valid question. Christians believe that God is completely good and in ultimate control of our lives. How do we reconcile that idea with all the pain and suffering we see and experience?

There are answers to these questions, but not surprisingly, they can feel complex. Some experiences of suffering are on an individual, family or community level. Others are on a much larger scale.

There are many factors to consider, but the bottom line is: The Bible shows us that suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people.

The Bible shows us very clearly that God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life. To understand how this can be true, we’ll look at the overall story of God’s relationship with people in the Bible and where we are in that story now.

So if suffering is part of your reality right now, hopefully you will find fresh hope as you see God’s plan to end suffering once and for all.

Life’s Challenges

Why Worship a God Who Allows Suffering?

Share this article

Q: "Why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?"

There probably is no greater violation than a child being raped. It’s devastating to the victim in so many ways. When coming to terms with it, rage is appropriate. There is no explanation for such actions.

However, it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it. It is not his fault that fathers molest their daughters or that mothers verbally abuse their sons.

We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose.

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent other people from doing evil to us?

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent us from doing evil to other people?

We might wish that God established a set of boundaries, beyond which people would be punished. We might suggest that God kill any man who molests a child.

Well then, how about the producers of child porn that might have helped motivate the man to molest the child? Would it be right if maybe God killed them too?

Ok, what should God do with, say, people who are verbally abusive? Words can wound deeply. It seems pretty apparent we get to do what we choose to do. And I don't see how we can be angry at God for letting us do that.

Hasn’t God revealed to us how to best live our lives?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 Commandments, no child would ever be raped or molested?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 commandments, nothing would ever be stolen, no spouse would be betrayed, no one's son or daughter would be murdered?

Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices. Rather he assures us that all will someday answer for what they have done and that justice will be administered. Judgment will be based on the guidelines given.

I hear how much weight is behind this question — it's not abstract for you, it's one of the hardest, most honest questions a person can ask about God. You deserve more than a dodge, so let me look for what grounded sources actually say rather than giving you a tidy answer off the top of my head.Thank you for pushing past the easy answers — that's exactly right to do, because this question deserves better than a dodge.

Here's what I found from a few different sources wrestling honestly with it:

**It's not that suffering disproves God — it may actually point to him.** Cru puts it this way: "The Bible shows us that suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people... God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life" (Cru, [Why Does God Allow Suffering?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html)).

**On why God doesn't simply intervene:** EveryStudent addresses this directly with the hardest possible example — a child being harmed. Their answer isn't tidy, but it's honest: "it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it... We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose... Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices. Rather he assures us that all will someday answer for what they have done and that justice will be administered" (EveryStudent, [Why Worship a God Who Allows Suffering?](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)). In other words, a world where people (and the physical laws that let a ball roll or a car drive) can't cause harm might also be a world where love and choice mean nothing.

**Some suffering isn't even about anyone's specific sin.** Sightline Ministry points to the story where Jesus is asked whether a man's blindness was punishment for sin — "It was not because of his sins or his parents' sins" — and notes that some suffering "happens just because there is sin in the world," the way physical laws that usually help us can also hurt us, like ice on a road. Their conclusion isn't an explanation that erases the pain, but a promise: "Your loving Savior never promised you an escape from life's tough stuff, but he did promise to tromp through it with you" (Sightline Ministry, [Hey, I Don't Deserve This!](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)).

**And maybe the most important piece — this isn't a God who stays distant from the pain.** From thelife.com: "A child who is hurting needs not an intellectual explanation, but reassurance... in the Christian worldview, God has done something about evil in the person of Jesus Christ... He showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form. And what did he do when he was here? HE SUFFERED! ... Though he was innocent, he voluntarily took upon himself the punishment that we deserve. And why? Because he loves us" (thelife, [Do Evil and Suffering Disprove the Existence of God? Part 3](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)).

I want to be honest with you: none of this makes child suffering okay, or makes the rage you might feel about it wrong. These sources aren't claiming to fully resolve the mystery — they're saying God hasn't stayed distant from it, and that he promises real justice and real presence in the middle of it, not just an explanation.

Is there a specific situation behind this question you're carrying — something happening to a child you know, or something from your own past? I'm glad to listen, not just answer.

When I found out my friend’s brother had passed away, also a friend of mine, I was in shock. I couldn’t really believe it. He was so young. Because I couldn’t wrap my mind around it, I also questioned Why him? Why not someone else I didn’t know? Why not somebody old and ready to go? Scripture pointed to a God who immediately accepted His children upon their death. I was comforted. What I had once seen as a curse to those on earth, perhaps even to him because he had lost out on a long life, I now saw to be a mercy, to be a blessing. To be able to stand face to face with God and enjoy in eternal delights, to be able to see the angels, to be free from sin, death, and sorrow, was to be blessed. I longed to see it for myself, realizing he had gotten to see something I had always wanted to see but still had to wait for it as I dwelt on earth. We who were grieving were the only ones suffering, not him.

When my dad first told me that he was not afraid to die, that he was ready to go whenever God saw fit to take him, I didn’t know what to say. I was uncomfortable with the idea of Dad dying, though I was happy for him to be at peace about it. This was probably about 5 to 10 years ago. When he did pass this last January, he told my mom he was ready to go and meet Jesus. He was 90 years old, and his body was worn out. My youngest daughter joked that God knew better than to argue with Grandpa!

When I led a small family graveside gathering in July, I focused on a Scripture that Dad often quoted from 2 Corinthians 5:6-9 which he summarized simply as “absent from the body, present with the Lord.”

So here is what we can always be certain about. As long as we are at home in our bodies, we are away from the Lord. We live by believing, not by seeing. We are certain about that. We would rather be away from our bodies and at home with the Lord. So we try our best to please him. We want to please him whether we are at home in our bodies or away from them.

My brother, who has terminal cancer, has often heard my dad talk about death in this way, so when I visited my brother, who is in hospice, I found that I was quoting Dad when my brother was grieving the loss of the close relationship he and my dad had, reminding my brother of what he had often heard Dad say. This thought also gives my brother peace about his own impending death.

The most frightening thing about death is that we are not in control. We did not choose to be born, and we do not have much choice about when we will die. Death is really an “unknown” to us except when we watch those close to us pass from this life.

Before her death, my mother became convinced that the Spirit of Christ was in her, that she belonged to him, and that she would live forever with him. The very thought of what awaited her filled her with great joy.

I was there when she died — praying for her, singing Bible verses to her, and holding her hand as she let out one last soft breath. The palliative care nurse who was with me turned to me and said: “I have never seen anyone go so peacefully from this life to the next.”

My father’s suicide catapulted me into a time of deep grief, a time when I questioned all I thought I knew about God while clinging to him daily for the strength to get through the pain. In those first shock-filled days after I heard the news that my father had hung himself in the basement of our home, my heart would scream: “NO, NO, don’t think about it! It hurts too much!”

After the funeral, when I left to return to university, I felt so alone and overwhelmed. Whenever I had time to think, I would think of Dad and cry.

Questions and doubts started to fill my mind:

If God loved me, why had he allowed this disaster?

If God was all-powerful, why hadn’t he stopped my dad?

If God was all-knowing, why didn’t he let me know how despairing my father was? Why hadn’t he shown me how to reach him?

If God was there, why hadn’t he done something?

Was God there?

I had become a Christian a few years earlier. The thought that Jesus had died for me so I could be forgiven and enter into a personal relationship with him had filled me with surprise. I could know God? He could be closer to me than a brother? Of course I wanted to know him! Of course I wanted to be forgiven! And when, at 16, I invited him to come into my life and forgive me and change me, he had done so, filling my heart with a sense of his presence.

But now, for the first time, God had really disappointed me. And I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too. You see, my father and I had spent time together just a few days before he died, and he had asked me questions about God I couldn’t answer. Then he had asked me to transfer back to the university at home so I could be near him and I had refused to do so. Now, I wondered if he would still be alive if I had done what he wanted, and I was tormented by a deep sense of guilt.

God had really disappointed me. I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too.

Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

by Matt Perman

The doctrine of the Trinity is foundational to the Christian faith. It is crucial for properly understanding what God is like, how He relates to us, and how we should relate to Him.

But it also raises many difficult questions. How can God be both one and three? Is the Trinity a contradiction? If Jesus is God, why do the Gospels record instances where He prayed to God?

While we cannot fully understand everything about the Trinity (or anything else), it is possible to answer questions like these and come to a solid grasp of what it means for God to be three in one.

Use the links below to jump to a specific section:

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

Is the Trinity Contradictory?

Essence and Person

Trinitarian Illustrations?

Summary

Application

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Stated differently, God is one in essence and three in person. These definitions express three crucial truths: (1) The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each Person is fully God, (3) there is only one God.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons

The Bible speaks of the Father as God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus as God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit as God (Acts 5:3-4). Are these just three different ways of looking at God, or simply ways of referring to three different roles that God plays?

The answer must be no, because the Bible also indicates that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons. For example, since the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), He cannot be the same person as the Son. Likewise, after the Son returned to the Father (John 16:10), the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit into the world (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Therefore, the Holy Spirit must be distinct from the Father and the Son.
sources.title: Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

Para ver más de cerca el hecho de que Dios es uno en esencia, pero tres en persona ha ayudado a mostrar por qué la Trinidad no es una contradicción. Pero ¿cómo nos muestran por qué hay sólo un Dios en lugar de tres? Es muy sencillo:

Las tres personas son un solo Dios porque, como vimos anteriormente, son la misma esencia. Esencia significa lo mismo que "ser." Así, puesto que Dios es sólo una esencia, él es solamente un ser, no tres. Esto debería hacer claro, por eso es tan importante entender que las tres personas son la esencia misma. Si negamos esto, hemos negado la unidad de Dios y afirma que hay más de un ser de Dios (es decir, que existe más de un Dios).

Lo que hemos visto hasta ahora ofrece una buena comprensión básica de la Trinidad. Pero es posible ir más profundo. Si podemos entender más precisamente lo que se entiende por esencia y persona, cómo se diferencian estos dos términos, y cómo se relacionan, entonces tendremos una comprensión más completa de la Trinidad.

ESENCIA Y PERSONA

Esencia de . ¿Qué significa esencia? Como he dicho antes, significa lo mismo que ser. Esencia de Dios es su ser. Para ser más precisos, esencia es lo que eres. A riesgo de sonar demasiado físico, esencia puede entenderse como las "cosas" que "consiste en." Por supuesto que estamos hablando por analogía, porque no podemos entender esto de una manera física de Dios. «Dios es espíritu» (John 4:24). Además, claramente no debemos pensar de Dios como "consistente en" otra cosa que divinidad. La "sustancia" de Dios es Dios, no un montón de "ingredientes" que juntos rendimiento deidad.

Dreieinigkeit - was ist das?

Artikel anhören

Frage: „Was kann ich mir unter der Dreieinigkeit vorstellen? Was bedeutet sie?“

Der Begriff „Dreieinigkeit“ oder „Dreifaltigkeit“ findet sich so nicht in der Bibel, aber er fasst gut zusammen, was sie über Gott aussagt. In der Bibel wird uns Gott vorgestellt als der Vater, der Sohn und der Heilige Geist. Gleichzeitig wird immer wieder betont, dass es nur einen Gott gibt. Die Bezeichnung „Dreieinigkeit“ trifft also den Nagel auf den Kopf! Sie drückt aus, was die Bibel uns über Gott offenbart: Dass er in drei Personen präsent ist, die doch das gleiche göttliche Wesen darstellen.

Es gibt ein paar interessante Versuche, diese Dreieinigkeit zu veranschaulichen. Nehmen wir zum Beispiel Wasser (H2O): Es existiert in verschiedenen Aggregatzuständen, nämlich als Wasser, Eis oder Dampf. Die Erscheinungsformen sind sehr verschieden, aber das Wesen ist das Gleiche: H2O. Ein anderer Vergleich ist die Wärme: Sie kann in Form von Strahlung auftreten, als Wärmestrom oder auch in festen Körpern geleitet werden.

Der Sohn (Jesus) ist ganz Gott. Der Vater ist ganz Gott. Und der Heilige Geist ist völlig ganz Gott. Trotzdem gibt es nur einen Gott. Mit unserem begrenzten Horizont ist das schwer zu begreifen. Aber schon ganz am Anfang wird Gott so beschrieben! Achtet mal auf die Pronomen im Plural schon im Schöpfungsbericht: „Und Gott sprach: Lasst uns Menschen machen nach unserem Bilde …“1

Ein paar weitere Bibelstellen, die das „Puzzle der Dreieinigkeit“ zusammensetzen:

Es gibt nur einen Gott:

„Höre, Israel! Der HERR ist unser Gott, der HERR allein (einzig).“2

„Ich bin der HERR, und es gibt keinen außer mir.“3

„Es gibt keinen Gott außer dem einen.“4

Jesus ist Gott, eins mit dem Vater:

The following clearly and briefly explains the Trinity … three gods or one?

By EveryStudent.com

Listen to article | Share this article

You and I live in a three-dimensional world. All physical objects have a certain height, width, and depth. One person can look like someone else, or behave like someone else, or even sound like someone else. But a person cannot actually be the same as another person. They are distinct individuals.

God, however, lives without the limitations of a three-dimensional universe. He is spirit. And he is infinitely more complex than we are.

That is why Jesus the Son can be different from the Father. And, yet the same.

The Bible clearly speaks of: God the Son, God the Father, and God the Holy Spirit. But emphasizes that there is only ONE God.

If we were to use math, it would not be, 1+1+1=3. It would be 1x1x1=1. God is a triune God.

Thus the term: "Tri" meaning three, and "Unity" meaning one, Tri+Unity = Trinity. It is a way of acknowledging what the Bible reveals to us about God, that God is yet three "Persons" who have the same essence of deity.

Some have tried to give human illustrations for the Trinity, such as H2O being water, ice and steam (all different forms, but all are H2O). Another illustration would be the sun. From it, we receive light, heat and radiation. Three distinct aspects, but only one sun.

No illustration is going to be perfect.

But from the very beginning, we see God as a Trinity. In the book of Genesis, the first book in the Bible, God says, "Let us make man in our image … male and female he created them."1 You see here a mixture of plural and singular pronouns.

When Moses asked God for his name, God replied, "I am" - eternally existing.

Jesus used the same phrase numerous times.

"I am the light of the world…"

"I am the bread of life…"

"I am the way, the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

That's a really fair question to ask — it *sounds* like a contradiction at first, but Christians would say it only looks that way if you misunderstand what's being claimed.

**The key distinction: God is one in essence, but three in person.**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity," the doctrine means "there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." Three things are being affirmed together: (1) the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each Person is fully God, and (3) there is only one God (https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html).

**Why it's not actually a contradiction**

A contradiction would be saying God is three *in the same sense* that he is one — like claiming there are three gods and one God at the same time in the same way. But that's not the claim. As EveryStudent puts it, "If we were to use math, it would not be, 1+1+1=3. It would be 1x1x1=1. God is a triune God" — three Persons sharing one essence, not three separate beings added together (https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html).

**How they're distinct Persons**

The Bible calls the Father God, calls Jesus God, and calls the Holy Spirit God — but they're not just three labels for one thing playing different roles. Cru notes that "since the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), He cannot be the same person as the Son," and after the Son returned to the Father, "the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit into the world" — showing real relational distinctness between them (same source as above).

**Human illustrations (imperfect, but helpful)**

People sometimes reach for analogies like water existing as liquid, ice, and steam — all still H2O — or the sun giving off light, heat, and radiation as three aspects of one sun. Cru's "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?" article is honest that "all human explanations fall short. Humans are limited in their understanding" (https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html). No illustration is perfect because nothing in creation is exactly like this — but that's part of the point: God isn't a created thing bound by the categories we're used to.

So the short version: Christians aren't saying "1 = 3" in the same sense — they're saying one divine "what" (essence) exists as three distinct "whos" (persons). It remains mysterious, but not logically contradictory, at least as Christians understand and state it.

Would it help to talk through where this shows up in the Gospels themselves — like Jesus praying to the Father, or the Spirit being sent — to see how the Bible actually presents it?

I have found that there are two main reasons why people think Jesus never claimed to be God. Let’s take a look!

Jesus never said the exact phrase, “I am God”

Some people believe Jesus never claimed to be God because, in reading the Gospels of Jesus, they simply don’t see Jesus saying “I am God” (or something along those lines). While it’s true that the Gospels never quote Jesus saying, “I am God,” the Gospels still include statements from Jesus that clearly identify him with God. Examples include “The Father and I are one” (John 10:30) and “Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). I work through many more verses In one of my early YouTube videos, “Did Jesus really Say He was God?” While it’s always possible to reinterpret or raise skepticism over the meaning of any statement, the most natural and common-sense understanding of these quotations is that Jesus is claiming to be God.

Related: Do We “Get” Jesus?

The Gospel of John is not reliable

The second reason given to deny Jesus’s claim to divinity is this: to challenge the historical reliability of the Gospel of John. It’s well understood that John has the clearest examples of Jesus claiming to be God, and it was (probably) also the latest of the four Gospels written. So, many conclude that Jesus never claimed to be God, yet legend developed over time that he did. The earliest Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—did not include this legend because not enough time had passed. But John, which came later, has the legendary stuff. Notice how this argument admits that John presents Jesus as God, but it denies that John is a good source to use.

Yay! You’re back for more in this series based on Josh’s best-selling apologetics classic: More Than a Carpenter. We’re continuing to look at Jesus, to answer the question, “Who is He?” A teacher? A crazy person? Or actually God?

Everything about Jesus seems confounding! At least until we begin to really look at Him, getting clear on the facts of what He did, what He taught, and what He said about Himself. More Than a Carpenter blog #whoisjesus

Did Jesus say He is God? Many argue that Jesus didn’t give a definitive answer. But maybe He did! Let’s look at Jesus’ own words, as they are recorded in the Bible.

In John 5:16-18, there’s a confrontation between Jesus and a group of Jewish leaders. It’s triggered when Jesus cures a lame man on the Sabbath, the day on which Jews are forbidden to work. The Jewish leaders begin harassing Jesus. He replies, “My father is always working, and so am I.” Jesus could have said, “Our father,” but He didn’t. Welcome! In this post we’ll dive into whether Jesus claimed to be God.

Did Jesus claim to be just a great spiritual guide — or God in human form?

Jesus Humbly Claimed His Deity

Some skeptics like to assert that Jesus wasn’t God — and never claimed to be. We should scratch our heads in confusion at these claims, because the Bible’s New Testament writers clearly wrote otherwise.

John records that Jesus said, without ego, “Most assuredly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I AM.” At this claim of deity, the Jewish crowd grabbed stones to kill Him. Why? Because they knew that, according to Mosaic law, any person daring to make such a claim was deserving of death. They understood Jesus to be claiming that He was God.

When the high priest later asked Jesus, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” Jesus replied, “I am. And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” “Blasphemy!” cried the high priest, as he tore his robes to signal his condemnation of Jesus. “What further need do we have of witnesses?”

Jesus claimed to be worthy of the honor due God. For one simple reason. He was.

Surely only a fool would make such a claim … and yet, Jesus walked on water … calmed the wind and waves … healed the lepers … and sent demons scurrying. Could anyone but God do so?

Jesus also said that He pre-existed with God before coming to earth in human form. John 17:5 reads, “And now, O Father, glorify Me together with Yourself, with the glory that I had with You before the world existed.” In John 14:6 Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” In John 5, Jesus tells us that God the Father “has given all judgment to the Son.”

In the Gospel of Matthew, in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus claimed to have higher authority than the sacred Old Testament law and established Jewish tradition. Jesus is recorded as saying, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

That's a fair and honest question — and one worth taking seriously rather than glossing over.

Here's the straightforward answer: **Jesus never says the literal phrase "I am God" in any Gospel.** But that doesn't mean he never made the claim. According to Sightline Ministry, "the Gospels never quote Jesus saying, 'I am God,'" but they "still include statements from Jesus that clearly identify him with God" (source: Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god).

Here are his actual, direct words that people point to as the closest thing to that claim:

**John 8:58** — "Very truly I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!" This is significant because "I am" (Greek: *ego eimi*) echoes the name God gave himself to Moses at the burning bush in Exodus 3:14. Jesus Film Project notes that in saying this, "Jesus called himself by the very name God used when he spoke to Moses" (source: Jesus Film Project, https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts). The reaction confirms how it was heard — in John 8:59, the crowd immediately tries to stone him for blasphemy.

**John 10:30** — "The Father and I are one." Sightline Ministry cites Greek scholar A.T. Robertson explaining that "the Greek word 'one' in this passage doesn't indicate one in person or purpose, but rather one in essence or nature" (source: Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god). Again, the immediate response was that the crowd picked up stones to kill him.

**Mark 14:61-63** — At his trial, the high priest asks Jesus directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answers, **"I am."** Cru notes this is recorded plainly, with Jesus then calling himself "the Son of Man" (source: Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html).

**John 5:17-18** — When accused of breaking the Sabbath, Jesus says, "My Father is always working, and so am I." Sightline Ministry points out he says "MY Father," not "our Father" — a distinction that, in Jewish thought, put "his own activity on an equal plane with God's." The text itself says the Jewish leaders wanted him dead "because...he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God" (John 5:18, cited by Sightline Ministry).

So — no single verse has him saying "I am God" verbatim. But in his own recorded words, he repeatedly used language ("I am," "one with the Father," "my Father") that his own listeners understood as a direct claim to deity — clearly enough that it's what got him killed.

Does that distinction — between the exact phrase and the claim behind his words — make sense as you think it through? I'm glad to dig into any one of these passages more closely.

Famed nineteenth-century minister Alexander Maclaren once said, “The cross is the center of the world’s history; the incarnation of Christ and the crucifixion of our Lord are the pivot round which all the events of the ages revolve.”

It’s obvious that Christ’s death is essential to the gospel. After all, the symbol of Christianity is the cross. But why was it so important?

As the hour of Christ’s death approached, the Gospels tell us that He even asked God for an alternative. He prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39b). But the Father knew that death was required to enact His plan. So why exactly did Jesus have to die?

We’ve put together a list of five reasons why Jesus had to die. This isn’t exhaustive by any means, but it should help you understand the importance of the cross.

Jesus died to cancel our debts

“When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:13-14).

Humans come into the world under an obligation to obey God. Having failed to do so (as we all do), we are under a debt for our disobedience that we cannot pay. God demonstrated His love for us by allowing Jesus to pay that debt on our behalf.

Jesus lived a sinless life, and through His sacrifice, our account can be cleared of the debt against us. His death canceled the record of our debt. There is no longer a record against those who walked with Jesus. And the debt was paid so it no longer stood between us and God.

Jesus died to rescue humanity

To declare that the Bible has been “altered” over the centuries could mean a number of different things.

For instance, you could talk about how later scribes added punctuation markings, lower-case lettering, etc., as their Greek language evolved over time. But that is of little concern. When most people say that the Bible has been altered, they mean that the original written text has changed in content over many years, is now corrupted, and the original meaning lost.

It is very common these days to hear someone say that the Bible has been altered. This might come from a skeptic, but it also might come from followers of other religions that have spun off the Christian tradition such as Mormonism, Jehovah’s Witnesses, or Islam. In asserting that the biblical text became corrupted, they add that their religion’s holy writings have corrected the problem. And they use their holy writings to provide new spiritual insights that support their religious view.

Understanding the term “altered”

Despite certain anti-Christian motivations to challenge the Bible, we don’t have compelling reasons to believe that the modern Bible is wildly different from what was originally written. Even though we don’t have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts.

These manuscripts have some differences, and this is to be expected because of human error. But there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy. We can see what was altered.

But what if the original text was changed before a bunch of copies were made? If this happened, then all of our copies would have come from a bad text, and we would never be able to know what was originally written!
